C5.evidence: The brief shows the real path: the first framing was 'shortage of healthcare access', it was narrowed to triage, a table records what was rejected and why (section 9), and section 12 lists what a real AI system would need. Honest limits are stated in section 6 and section 11. Stack is named: Python, Streamlit, Pandas, Plotly. Your commit history shows Cursor was used (the commit 'Add CarePath Streamlit triage prototype' has a Cursor co-author line), but the brief does not say so.
C5.gap: No bug or failed attempt is described. The testing section (section 10) lists 3 expected pathways and says they 'demonstrate that the intended decision pathways are implemented'. That claim is not true of the live app for typed answers. No next-step dates or owners beyond a roadmap.
C5.action: Add a 'What broke' section that reports the typed-answers bug, the screenshot of the 0% result, the fix you made, and the date you re-tested, and name Cursor as the AI tool you used with what you used it for.

C6.evidence: Your statement is specific: you want to turn real problems into practical technology that fits the Nigerian context. The portfolio shows about two dozen public repos from before the sprint, including a voice-first AI tutor, a health dashboard and a hackathon tool. The entry itself shows effort: presets, a clinician handoff download, a Pidgin option, a contribution chart, and a 16-section brief with references.
C6.gap: The statement does not name a TIC project you want to lead. It is strong on what you will learn and gain, and less strong on what you will build for the club.
C6.action: Name one TIC project you want to lead this term (for example a Pidgin voice version of CarePath for a PHC), and say which of your earlier repos you would bring to it.

entries.verdict: You have a well-argued, honest triage design and a live app whose preset cases work, but a typed-in danger sign is lost before the result, so a real user with seizure and confusion would be told to monitor at home.
entries.strongestPoint: Your design reasoning is the clearest part of the entry: a written table of rejected options (ML model now, diagnosis, many diseases, backend), with the reason for each, and the brief says plainly that the weights are not clinical thresholds.
entries.biggestGap: Typed-in answers never reach the result. Ticking seizure and confusion by hand gives 'Monitor and reassess' with 0% completeness, which is the most serious gap in this entry.
improvements: Copy every answer into a plain dictionary when the user presses Continue, so the symptom and danger-sign values reach the result page, then test the typed seizure and confusion case.
Add a 'What broke' section that shows the typed-answers bug with a screenshot, the fix, and the date you re-tested.
Test 3 existing symptom checkers on the same 5 cases and write down where each one differs from CarePath.

entries.name: Nicholas Onuorah
entries.title: danfo

C1.evidence: Your game puts the player at 'OJOTA BUS STOP, 9:14am' with a sister's wedding in Lekki by 11am, a Bolt fare of NGN 4,200 because of surge, and 'Your data dey also finish small small'. The setting and the constraints are specific. Your brief says only that you 'thought about my area and what some people go through'. It never says who the player is.
C1.gap: You name a setting and real constraints, but no real person and no root cause. The next band needs the user written down (for example a worker who must reach Lekki on time with little money) and the cost, data or traffic problem explained as a real problem, not only as a joke in the game.
C1.action: Write three lines about one real person you know who made a Lagos trip like this in the last month: their route, what it cost them, and how long it took.

C2.evidence: Your brief names no source, no survey and no existing game. It describes choosing Rust and debugging with help. The Lagos details in the game (Ojota, Third Mainland, Bolt surge, okada, a police checkpoint) come from your own knowledge with no check against any source.
C2.gap: No research is shown. The next band needs a few cited claims, such as a published danfo or Bolt fare with its source and date, or a primary check where you asked real people.
C2.action: Ask five people who travel to Lekki what they paid last week for a danfo, an okada and a Bolt, and write the five answers in your brief.

C3.evidence: Your brief gives one reason: 'I chose this to well be able to understand it ... since its in my curriculum', which is a reason for the language. It gives no reason for the game design. It does not say why the game is text, why time and cash are the two stats, or why the routes are set up as they are.
C3.gap: You describe the scenes and endings but do not justify them. The next band needs a stated design decision with a reason, and at least one thing you chose not to build.
C3.action: Write one paragraph that explains why you chose a text game over a graphic one, why time and cash are the two stats, and name one feature you left out and why.

C4.evidence: The code is public at github.com/nicholaswashere-ops/nicholas12345 in rust/danfo/src/main.rs (347 lines). We read the source on GitHub and did not run it. The choices change cash, time and vibe, route to other scenes, and reach one of four endings. The game is a real branching game with Lagos scenes and Pidgin dialogue. But there is no hosted or browser version, the README is only the repo name, and a reviewer needs a Rust toolchain (edition 2024) before they can play it. The time limit cannot run out. The start time is 90 minutes (line 40). The largest total time cost on any route is 41 minutes (-25 on the danfo, -6 in the danfo scene, -10 at the conductor scene), so the 'YOU MISSED THE ENTRY DANCE' ending (line 258) cannot be reached. The Bolt option costs NGN 4,200 (line 172) and the player starts with NGN 2,500. The code clamps cash to 0 (line 65) instead of blocking the purchase.
C4.gap: To reach the next band, the time limit must be able to run out, and an unaffordable option must be blocked. A reviewer also needs a way to play without a toolchain, such as a README with exact run steps or a browser build. The stakes are the heart of a game, and right now the player cannot lose on time.
C4.action: Change the start time on line 40 from 90 to 40, play the danfo route once, and confirm the missed-entry ending appears.

C5.evidence: Your brief lists steps: you chose Rust, 'proofread and debugged with assist', 'stored it as a sublime text' and 'ran it in my command prompt'. It names no bug and no change. The brief is 481 bytes long.
C5.gap: The steps are listed, but there is no problem, no iteration and no decision. 'With assist' does not say which AI tool helped or what it changed. The next band needs at least one real bug you hit and the tool that helped you fix it.
C5.action: Name one bug you hit while building (for example the Bolt cost or the time check), say which AI tool you asked for help, and write what you changed.

C6.evidence: Your statement is sincere but general: you want to make a positive difference for yourself and PAU. Your repo shows Rust practice before the sprint. It has a practice crate, and the first commits are dated 30 August 2026, before the sprint started. That is evidence of past building.
C6.gap: Your statement does not say what you want to build or do in TIC. The next band needs a specific purpose and a finished project you can show a user. Your danfo game is not yet a finished project a user can open.
C6.action: Write one sentence that names the game you want to build for TIC next term and the TIC session you would join to start it.

entries.verdict: You built a real branching Rust text game with specific Lagos scenes and Pidgin, but the time limit cannot run out and a reviewer cannot play it without installing Rust.
entries.strongestPoint: The Lagos scenes (Ojota bus stop, Third Mainland, Bolt surge, okada, a police checkpoint) and the Pidgin dialogue are specific, and each choice changes the game state and the route.
entries.biggestGap: The time limit cannot run out. The worst route costs 41 of the 90 minutes, so the main stake of the game does not exist, and the missed-entry ending cannot be reached.
improvements: Change the start time on line 40 of rust/danfo/src/main.rs from 90 to 40, play the danfo route once, and confirm the missed-entry ending appears.
Block the Bolt option when cash is below NGN 4,200, then check that a player with NGN 2,500 cannot buy it.
Add a README to rust/danfo with the exact cargo run steps and the Rust version needed, and remove the committed .exe, .pdb and target/ folders from the repo.

entries.name: Chinedu Mbaeto
entries.title: A Farm Traceability Website

C1.evidence: The uploaded brief file is the app's source code (2,147 lines of HTML, CSS and JavaScript), so it holds no problem statement. The only framing is on the page: 'Connect farmers, buyers and supply-chain partners through transparent batch records'. That restates the stream topic. The sample farms are in Ethiopia and Switzerland, and prices are in US dollars.
C1.gap: You name no user, no place and no constraint. Nothing in the design shows a Nigerian farmer or buyer. Band 8 to 11 needs one specific user in one specific setting, with one real limit that shapes the design.
C1.action: Write one paragraph that names one Nigerian farmer, one buyer, the market they trade in, and one constraint they face (for example, buyers cannot check a price before they travel).

C2.evidence: We found no research in the uploaded file or the repo. The sample farms, the certifier names (for example 'AgriCert Standard Labs') and the prices are invented. No source, statistic or competitor is named.
C2.gap: You show no research at all. Band 4 to 7 needs a few sourced claims. Band 8 to 11 needs those sources plus a look at existing traceability tools and what they miss.
C2.action: List three existing produce marketplaces or traceability tools, and write one line on what each does and one line on what it misses for a farmer.

C3.evidence: The page has four sections (Marketplace, Traceability, Farmer Portal, Dashboard). The header says 'Simulated Web3 Node' and the mint form says 'simulated on-chain provenance record', which is an honest label. The code keeps all data in the browser's localStorage. The brief does not say why a blockchain-style ledger was chosen, why browser storage was chosen, or what stops a fake farm from registering.
C3.gap: You describe features but do not justify them. You do not compare a simulated ledger with a normal database. You do not consider how a Nigerian farmer with weak connectivity would use the app, and the product photos load from an external image host. The main risk, that anyone can mint a batch under any farm name, is not named.
C3.action: Write a three-row decisions table: why a ledger or not, why browser storage or not, and what stops a fake farm from registering. For each row, give the reason and the risk you accept.

C4.evidence: The public link (lovable.dev/projects/df880672-602b-45ed-b6e8-29f31afe01c6) shows 'You don't have access. This project is private.' We clicked the page's 'Log in' button, which opened the Lovable login page. We entered no details and did not request access. The prototype could not be used by a public reviewer, so there was nothing to test live. We do not run entrant code, so we read the uploaded source only. It shows a marketplace, a traceability search and a mint form in JavaScript, with data kept in localStorage.
C4.gap: A reviewer cannot open the prototype, so this score stays in the 0 to 7 band. The source also shows that the verification is for display only. Every product card prints 'Verified Origin' and every batch searched shows 'On-Chain Verified', whether it was minted seconds ago or not. 'Units listed' counts batches, not units. The cart is a counter with no checkout and no way to remove an item. The next band needs a link any reviewer can open, where the verification works for real.
C4.action: Publish the Lovable project to a public URL, open that URL in a private browser window with no login, and send us the link.

C5.evidence: The uploaded brief file is source code, not a process brief. It has no steps, no problems hit, no iterations and no AI tool named. The processDocLink field in your entry is empty.
C5.gap: No process is shown. Band 3 to 5 needs the steps you took. Band 6 to 8 needs what broke, what you changed, and which tools (including AI tools) you used for which part.
C5.action: Write a one-page process note in time order: what you tried first, what broke, what you changed, and which AI tool you used for which part.

C6.evidence: Your statement says you want to improve and relearn skills you already have. It names no TIC role or project. Your public repo has one small 2025 upload. The prototype file was committed after the deadline.
C6.gap: The statement is generic, and the repo shows no past building. Band 6 to 8 needs a named TIC role or project you want to work on, or a link to earlier work you can show.
C6.action: Link one earlier project you built yourself, and name one TIC project you will lead in the first term.

entries.verdict: You submitted a one-page demo that labels every batch as verified without any check behind the label, and a reviewer could not open it at all, and it arrived about an hour after the deadline.
entries.strongestPoint: The mint form checks required fields, and the code escapes user text before it reaches the page (escapeHTML), so a farmer typing HTML cannot break the layout.
entries.biggestGap: The verified claims are not real. Every batch shows 'Verified Origin' and 'On-Chain Verified', and anyone can mint a batch under any farm name. A public reviewer also could not open the prototype.
improvements: Publish the Lovable project to a public URL and test it yourself in a private browser window with no login.
Make the verified label earn its name: show 'Verified' only for batches that a second party has checked, and store who checked and when.
Move the app to Nigerian data: naira prices, Nigerian sample farms, and a quantity field with a number and a unit (kg or tonnes) so buyers can add up totals.

entries.name: Dami Fakiyesi
entries.title: PowerGuard: Solving power and grid management issues in nigeria

C1.evidence: Your brief says 'users need to understand how much energy their appliances consume and how that affects electricity costs and available power.' The tariff is set in naira per kWh, the only Nigeria-specific detail.
C1.gap: The user is 'users' or 'households', with no place, no size and no income or setting. The naira tariff is an input the user types in. It does not change the design.
C1.action: Name one real user (for example, a provision shop owner in Surulere with a fridge and a freezer on an inverter) and write their monthly bill, outage hours per day and battery size into the brief.

C2.evidence: The brief has no figures, no sources and no existing product. The tariff is typed in by the user, not taken from a published source.
C2.gap: You have no sourced claims at all. Band 4 to 7 needs a few sourced statistics, and band 8 to 11 needs a comparison with existing solutions.
C2.action: Look up the current tariff for your local electricity distributor (DisCo) on its website, cite the page and date, and set that number as the default tariff in the app.

C3.evidence: The brief sets four battery modes (NORMAL at 80 percent and above, MODERATE at 50 to 79, SAVING at 20 to 49, CRITICAL below 20) and says lower-priority appliances are cut first. It gives the reason: 'available power becomes limited'.
C3.gap: The brief does not explain why 80, 50 and 20 were chosen, what happens to a fridge or freezer when it is cut, or what alternative design you rejected. No risk is named.
C3.action: Pick a battery datasheet, write one sentence on why the 20 percent critical line protects the battery, and one sentence on what happens to a fridge that is switched off at that level.

C4.evidence: The console app (Program.cs) asks for appliance name, watts, hours, tariff and priority, then calculates energy as W / 1000 x hours and cost as energy x tariff (checked in the code). It saves records to usage_history.txt. Its battery section cuts the lowest-priority appliance at 50 percent or less, and cuts all of them below 20 percent. The WinForms dashboard (Form1.cs lines 12 to 15) hard-codes batteryLevel = 75, energyUsed = 6.5 and tariff = 200, and its 'Automatic Switch System' panel is a fixed label.
C4.gap: The console works from start to finish, but it crashes on bad input (Convert.ToDouble and Convert.ToInt32 throw), and it sheds load but never switches a source. The dashboard is one static screen. PowerGuardCore is referenced by the project files, but no code calls it. There is no README, screenshot or test project, so a reviewer must install .NET 10 and guess what to type.
C4.action: Replace the Convert.ToDouble and Convert.ToInt32 calls in Program.cs with double.TryParse and int.TryParse inside a re-ask loop, then type 'abc' for watts and confirm the program asks again instead of crashing.

C5.evidence: Your process brief lists eleven build steps in order: console calculator, multiple appliances, history file, appliance class, battery modes, priorities, shared core, then dashboard. It names C#, .NET and VS Code.
C5.gap: No problem, failed attempt or change after a test is recorded, and the brief does not say whether AI tools were used. Two claims go beyond the repo: step 11 says the dashboard is connected to PowerGuardCore, and section 6 says tests covered the AC, fridge and microwave cases. No code references PowerGuardCore and there is no test project.
C5.action: Add a 'What broke' step with one real bug you hit (for example, the console crash on bad input) and what you changed, and remove the claim about the core connection unless you wire it up.

C6.evidence: Your statement says you want to learn more about embedded systems and machine learning, and gives networking and opportunities as reasons. You have no portfolio link, and the repo has two commits in the sprint window.
C6.gap: You name no TIC project or role, and you link no past build. The statement is sincere, but it could be written by anyone in the club.
C6.action: Name one TIC stream or role you want and one thing you would build for it next term, then link one public repo you built before the sprint.

entries.verdict: A working console calculator with real battery-mode logic, let down by a dashboard that shows fixed numbers and a brief that claims a core connection and tests the repo does not contain.
entries.strongestPoint: The console app does real arithmetic, saves a usage history and sheds the lowest-priority load first, and the battery bands are written out clearly.
entries.biggestGap: The dashboard is a static screen with hard-coded values, and the brief says it is connected to the core logic, which the repo does not show.
improvements: Replace the Convert.ToDouble and Convert.ToInt32 calls in Program.cs with TryParse and a re-ask loop, then type 'abc' for watts to confirm the app does not crash.
Make Form1.cs read batteryLevel and the appliance states from PowerGuardCore, then delete the hard-coded values.
Add a test project with one test that checks 1000 W for 2 hours at 200 naira per kWh gives 2 kWh and 400 naira, and cite that test in the brief.

entries.name: Chika Nwaezeigwe
entries.title: Voltra: Monitoring your power.

C1.evidence: Your brief says the dashboard 'summarizes the power situation in ones living space' and that Manual mode is 'the recommended mode for end users'. It names the unstable supply in Nigeria as the problem. It does not name a place, a household type or a daily pattern.
C1.gap: The user is 'one's living space' and 'end users'. No hostel, flat or shop is named in the brief. The 200 V and 250 V cut-offs shape the whole design, but the brief never explains them.
C1.action: Pick one hostel room or shop, log its mains voltage for one day with a cheap meter, and put the lowest and highest readings in the first paragraph of the brief.

C2.evidence: The brief has no figure, no source and no product. Its only research claim is 'the unstable power supply in Nigeria'. The live page cites nothing either.
C2.gap: No sourced statistic and no existing product are named. Band 4 to 7 needs a few sourced claims, and band 8 to 11 needs a comparison with a product that exists.
C2.action: Find one published figure for mains voltage swings or outage hours in a Nigerian city, cite it with a link and date, and name one voltage stabiliser and one thing it lacks.

C3.evidence: The live page shows the rules: 'Grid low < 200V, Grid high > 250V, Solar ready >= 12V'. Its status text explains one choice: 'Grid fault, but the solar bank is not charged enough yet, staying on grid'. The brief explains none of these rules.
C3.gap: You do not say why 200 V and 250 V are the cut-offs, why 12 V is the solar-ready level, or what a fridge or laptop does at 260 V. You compare no alternative, such as a generator, and name no risk.
C3.action: Add three sentences to the brief: why 200 V and 250 V were chosen, why 12 V counts as solar ready, and which appliance each rule protects.

C4.evidence: The live site at voltra.vercel.app loads with no login. In Manual mode, grid 180 V with solar 24 V moved to 'Solar Active'. Grid 180 V with solar 5 V stayed on 'Grid Active' and showed the reason. Grid 280 V with solar 24 V moved to solar with 'running on solar to protect the load'. In Demo mode the grid read 274.3 V and then 156.2 V, ten seconds apart. The mobile layout is clean.
C4.gap: The Live view should show your circuit, but it shows a shared web store. The public history holds 60 readings, all from Manual or Demo mode, and none from a device. Anyone can post to that feed, and the device API key sits in the public JavaScript. The page logs a download-button fetch error and a WebSocket close on load. The dashboard measures voltage only: no kW, kWh, battery or generator, so 'power' in the name is not measured. To reach 26, Live must show readings from your ESP32 only, the POST route must reject posts without a device key, and the load errors must be fixed.
C4.action: Add a device key check to the POST /api/reading route and filter the Live view to readings from your ESP32's device ID, then test that a POST without the key is rejected.

C5.evidence: Your brief covers Sense, Think and Act, the three modes and the Wokwi circuit. It says 'I used AI to assist me in the code and how best to wire the components of the circuitry.' That is an honest answer, and it is rewarded here.
C5.gap: The brief records no failed attempt, no problem and no change. It says the dashboard 'had to be connected to the circuitry over wifi, to get real time changes'. The live app has no device data, and the sketch image in your brief has no Wi-Fi code. The process brief claims a link that is not shown.
C5.action: Write a 'What went wrong' section with two items, then either show the ESP32 Wi-Fi code and one real post to your live app, or remove the Wi-Fi claim from the brief.

C6.evidence: Your statement says you want to build something of your own that helps people. Your brief says you are new to embedded systems. You link no portfolio and no past project.
C6.gap: The statement names no problem, no TIC role and no feature you want to build. It shows no past build. Band 6 to 8 needs a specific contribution you want to make and a link to past work.
C6.action: Name one power problem you want to solve for TIC next term and link one past project, even a school or Arduino tutorial build with a photo.

entries.verdict: A working voltage-switching dashboard with clear modes, held back by a Live view that shows shared web data instead of your circuit, and a brief that claims a Wi-Fi link that the evidence does not show.
entries.strongestPoint: The switching rule is real. In every Manual test the page did what its thresholds say: 180 V with solar 24 V moved to solar, and 180 V with solar 5 V stayed on grid with a reason.
entries.biggestGap: On the live site, the Live view shows values posted from the web page, not from a circuit, and the write route accepts posts from anyone.
improvements: Add a device key check to the POST route, and filter the Live view to readings from your ESP32 only.
Explain the 200 V, 250 V and 12 V rules in your brief, with the appliance each rule protects.
Add a measured or simulated current input so the dashboard shows watts, not only volts, and say in the brief how it is produced.

entries.name: Andikan-Phoebe Gideon Etefia
entries.title: FraudShield NG

C1.evidence: Your 'Problem' section repeats the stream brief almost word for word: 'Millions of unsophisticated internet users are losing their livelihoods to complex phishing and local 419 digital tactics'. The user is 'Millions of unsophisticated internet users', with no place, job, or setting from your own research.
C1.gap: The problem is named, but the user is generic. Band 8 to 11 needs one specific user in one setting, with one real constraint. The low-literacy constraint from the stream brief does not shape anything you describe in your own words.
C1.action: Pick one user (for example a Lagos trader who gets bank and mobile money SMS on a basic phone) and write one paragraph that says what that user reads, what they cannot read easily, and what the first line of your tool must say to them.

C2.evidence: Your brief has no sources and no statistics. It names no existing scam checker and no test with a real user. We did not find any research in the brief beyond the Rust code screenshot, which is a build artefact.
C2.gap: You show that you wrote a tool, but not what the fraud problem looks like for real people. Band 4 to 7 needs a few sourced claims. Band 8 to 11 needs a cited source and a look at an existing product.
C2.action: Collect 10 real scam messages from people you know (with their permission), sort them into 3 groups by type, and put the counts and the group names in your brief.

C3.evidence: Your brief names two limits: 'It uses predefined fraud indicators' and 'It does not work for all scam messages or as a complete scam message detector'. You use three risk levels, High Risk, Caution and Low Risk, and show a warning sign list for each message.
C3.gap: You do not explain why you chose these levels, these indicators, or a web page over a USSD or SMS format. The live page marks a real bank OTP notice as High Risk, and your brief does not name that as a false alarm. Your brief does not discuss cost or how a user without data would reach the tool.
C3.action: Test the tool on 5 real bank OTP notices and 5 real scam messages, count the false alarms and the misses, and write one paragraph that names the false alarm risk and the change you would make.

C4.evidence: The live app at fraudshield-ng-alert.lovable.app loads with no login. The check runs in the browser with 12 weighted patterns. We tested your brief's example ('Your BVN has been blocked. Send your OTP to 08031234567 to unblock now') and got High Risk with 5 warning signs. 'Hi mum, I will be home by 6' got Low Risk. The Pidgin message 'Abeg send me your account number and OTP' got High Risk. Each warning sign has a plain-language reason, and five example buttons fill the box in one tap.
C4.gap: Four faults showed up in our tests. First, 'Your OTP is 482913. Do not share it with anyone. - GTBank' gets High Risk, because any match on OTP forces High Risk, so a real bank notice gets the same alarm as a scam. Second, 'Your transfer has been verified' gets an 'asks you to verify' sign, because the pattern matches the letters 'verif'. Third, the verdict and the sign list disagree: 'Your GTBank account has been debited N1,500' lists a bank-impersonation sign and still gets Low Risk. Fourth, 'Hi mum, I will be home by 6. Pls send me N500 for food' gets Low Risk, so a money request is not flagged. There is no Pidgin option, no voice, and no USSD or SMS path. To reach the next band, the OTP rule needs context, the verdict and signs must agree, and the page needs a voice or language option.
C4.action: Stop the OTP pattern from forcing High Risk on its own: give it 2 points instead, then test 'Your OTP is 482913. Do not share it with anyone. - GTBank' and write the verdict you get in your brief.

C5.evidence: Your brief names the tools you used (a Rust program, ChatGPT and Lovable), says you 'know little to nothing when it comes to coding', and embeds four images, several of them Rust code in Sublime Text. It names two limits of the tool. This is an honest account of how the tool was made.
C5.gap: The brief does not say what broke, or what you changed after a test. The live page does not run the Rust keyword list from your screenshot. It runs 12 JavaScript patterns, and the brief does not say the logic was rewritten. Band 9 to 10 needs the full path plus a next-step plan.
C5.action: Add a 'What broke and what changed' section that compares the 17-item Rust keyword list with the 12 patterns on the live page, and name the two bugs that led to the change.

C6.evidence: Your statement says you want more exposure to real-world technology, and you are not yet sure what to build. The portfolio field is empty, and no repo is linked.
C6.gap: The statement is sincere but general. It names no TIC role and no project, and no past work is shown. Band 6 to 8 needs a specific contribution or a link to past work.
C6.action: Link the folder or repo for your Rust project, and name one TIC project you want to help build in the first term.

entries.verdict: You built a working browser checker with plain-language reasons, but a real bank OTP notice gets High Risk, and your brief does not say the logic was rewritten from the Rust code.
entries.strongestPoint: The page works with no login and explains each warning sign in plain words. Your brief is open about how little coding you knew and which AI tools you used.
entries.biggestGap: The OTP pattern forces High Risk on any message that mentions OTP, so a real bank notice gets the same alarm as a scam.
improvements: Give the OTP pattern 2 points instead of forcing High Risk, then test 'Your OTP is 482913. Do not share it with anyone. - GTBank' and record the verdict in your brief.
Fix the money pattern so 'send me N500' is flagged, and stop the verification pattern matching 'verified' by using whole-word matches.
Add a 'What broke and what changed' section that covers the move from Rust to the web page and the two bugs above, and name the tool you used for each fix.

entries.name: Nickson Omoike
entries.title: Rush Hour Traffic

C1.evidence: Your brief describes a 'high-score road-dodging game' with a 'lane-based car' on 'an endless road'. It names no player, no place and no problem. It does not mention Nigeria, Africa or a danfo or matatu. The live game is titled 'MATATU RUSH' and its text is in English only.
C1.gap: You have a mechanic but no user and no problem. The next band needs a named player and a setting (for example a commuter who takes a danfo to school in Lagos at 7am) and one real constraint that shapes the design.
C1.action: Write three sentences: who plays this game, where and when they play it, and what it should make them feel about the daily commute.

C2.evidence: Your brief and statement show no research. There is no source, no survey, no interview and no look at another game. The brief's only background is the mechanic itself.
C2.gap: Nothing is researched. The next band needs at least a few sourced claims, or a primary check such as a short ride-along or a short survey of people who commute.
C2.action: Ride a danfo for 30 minutes at rush hour, write down the three things that happened most often (for example stops, lane changes, hawkers), and put that list in your brief.

C3.evidence: Your brief explains some choices. The timing minigame 'sets starting time budget', checkpoints 'grant bonus time', and you used 'PNGs as objects' 'due to limits'. The live game does what the brief says: a start lock at the centre of the bar gave 45 s, and a lock at the edge gave 30 s.
C3.gap: You describe features but do not weigh them. Why a timing minigame and not a free start? What does a new player lose if the time budget is too tight? The next band needs one trade-off you made and one risk you handled, for example phone data cost or a slow phone.
C3.action: Write one paragraph that explains why the start-time bar exists, and what a new player should expect from a 30-second start, and say whether you tested it with anyone.

C4.evidence: The link https://rush-traffic-dodge-081941.onhercules.app/ loads with no login. We played about nine rounds with real steering, pause and restart. The clock counts down in real time, and 'Time's up!' with 'JOURNEY OVER' appears when it reaches zero. The start-time bar gave 45 s at the centre and 30 s at the edge, as your brief says. At phone width (390x844) the layout and the on-screen controls appear. Three things kept this out of the next band. First, a truck hit costs about 1 second and gives no visible feedback. In one screenshot the car sits on a truck and the score keeps rising. Second, the first two ArrowLeft presses after the start lock did not move the car. Third, we did not reach the finish line, and one restart showed the same figures as the earlier round, so we could not confirm that a new round started. We also did not see a checkpoint on screen, although your brief says they grant bonus time. The obstacle sprites sit on white and grey boxes, and the game text has no Nigerian place, language or event. 'Matatu' is the word used in Kenya and East Africa, and Nigerians say danfo.
C4.gap: To reach the next band, a hit must be clear to the player, the first controls must respond straight away, a restart must clearly start a new round, and the checkpoints must be visible. The Nigerian content must also appear in the game itself, not only in the title. The obstacle boxes are the first thing a reviewer sees as unfinished.
C4.action: Add a red screen flash and a clock penalty of 3 seconds on each vehicle hit, then play three rounds and check that the penalty shows on the clock each time.

C5.evidence: Your brief says you used 'an Ai application' to build a web React app and that you 'had to outsource my work to an Ai agent due to a tight time schedule'. It is honest about the limits: 'a lot of bugs have currently not been optimized' and the mobile version is 'not fully ... optimized'.
C5.gap: The brief is honest about the limits, but it does not list what broke, what you tried, or what changed. It does not name the AI tool. The next band needs one bug, the fix you tried, and the tool used for it.
C5.action: Write down three bugs you know about (for example the hit with no feedback and the first controls that do not respond), and for each one write the fix you asked the AI agent for and whether it worked.

C6.evidence: Your statement says you want to create games for others to enjoy. No portfolio or repo is linked, and no earlier project is shown.
C6.gap: The statement is sincere but general. It names no TIC role and no past build. The next band needs one specific thing you want to build or contribute, and evidence that you have built something before.
C6.action: Link one earlier project (a GitHub repo, a Scratch project or a live page) in the portfolio field, or write plainly that this is your first build.

entries.verdict: You built a working browser arcade game with a real timing start, a countdown and a clear end state, but it has no Nigerian content, and a reviewer sees unfinished details such as the box behind each vehicle.
entries.strongestPoint: The core loop works end to end in the browser: the start-time bar sets your clock, steering and speed change your progress, and the round ends with a score and a Try Again button.
entries.biggestGap: The game has no Nigerian or African content beyond the word in the title, and your brief does not describe a player or a problem, so the stream's cultural goal is not met.
improvements: Add a red flash and a 3-second clock penalty on each vehicle hit, then play three rounds and check the penalty shows each time.
Put one Lagos detail in the game itself, such as a danfo conductor line or a Lagos road name on the title screen, and call the minibus a danfo instead of a matatu.
Write three sentences that name the player, the place and the problem the game is about, and add them to the top of your brief.
